summary: Specifies version 4 of the Internet Message Access Protocol, which lets a client access and manipulate email messages on a server, including remote folders, much like local mailboxes. It also supports offline clients. It was replaced by RFC 2060 and RFC 2061.

plainLanguage.summary: Your email stays on the mail computer and you view and sort it from anywhere, like a filing cabinet you open remotely.

questions: how to fetch email with imap
subtitle: Protocol for accessing and managing email messages on a server.

tldr.problem: Users want to access their email from multiple devices without downloading all messages to each device, while still being able to manage folders and check for new messages.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4 provides a client-server protocol where messages stay on the server and clients can read, search, and manipulate them over a network connection.
tldr.outcome: IMAP4 became widely deployed but was refined and updated by RFC 2060 and RFC 2061, which provide better compatibility and additional features.

today: RFC 1730 is a Proposed Standard that has been superseded by RFC 2060 and RFC 2061, which provide updated and clarified specifications for IMAP4. Most IMAP4 implementations conform to the later RFCs.

sections.title: What is IMAP4
sections.content:
IMAP4 (Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4) is a network protocol that lets a client access and manipulate electronic mail messages stored on a server. Unlike protocols that download messages to the client, IMAP4 allows clients to read and manage messages while they remain on the server.

The protocol supports creating, deleting, and renaming mailboxes (message folders), checking for new messages, setting message flags, searching for specific messages, and selective downloading of message content. Messages are identified by either a sequence number (position in the mailbox) or a unique identifier (UID) that never changes, even if other messages are deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP is a way to read email that stays on a server. You ask the server what messages you have, and it tells you, then you pick which ones to read instead of downloading everything.

sections.title: Protocol States and Connection Flow
sections.content:
An IMAP4 session moves through four states. The Non-Authenticated State is entered when a client first connects. The client must provide valid credentials using the LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE command to enter the Authenticated State.

From Authenticated State, the client must select a mailbox using the SELECT or EXAMINE command to enter the Selected State, where messages can be read and modified. The CLOSE command or failed selection returns to Authenticated State. The Logout State is entered via the LOGOUT command, and the server closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to IMAP, it starts by asking for your password (non-authenticated). Once you prove who you are (authenticated), you pick a folder (selected), and then you can read and sort mail. When done, you log out.

sections.title: Client Commands and Message Identifiers
sections.content:
Client commands are prefixed with a tag—an alphanumeric string like A0001 or A0002—that identifies each command uniquely. The server echoes this tag in its completion response so the client knows which command succeeded or failed.

The FETCH command retrieves message data, including headers, body text, or just specific parts. The SEARCH command finds messages matching criteria like sender, date, or keywords. The STORE command sets message flags (like seen, answered, or deleted). The UID command variant allows using message unique identifiers instead of sequence numbers, which is safer when messages are deleted in other sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request gets a label (a tag) so the server knows which reply goes with which request. You can ask for specific messages by number or by unique ID, and you can search for messages by who sent them or when.

sections.title: Mailbox Organization and Operations
sections.content:
The CREATE, DELETE, and RENAME commands manage mailboxes. The LIST command returns all mailboxes on the server with their attributes (such as whether they accept messages or contain subfolders). The LSUB command returns only the subscribed mailboxes, which is the list of folders the user has chosen to follow.

The SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE commands let clients add or remove mailboxes from their personal subscription list. The APPEND command adds a new message to a mailbox. The EXPUNGE command permanently removes messages marked with the \Deleted flag.
sections.plainLanguage: You can create new folders, delete old ones, rename them, and say which folders you pay attention to. You can also add messages to a folder or permanently throw away messages marked for deletion.

sections.title: Server Responses and Data Exchange
sections.content:
The server sends two types of responses: tagged responses prefixed with the command's tag (indicating command completion with status OK, NO, or BAD), and untagged responses prefixed with an asterisk. Untagged responses include mailbox status (number of existing or recent messages), search results, or message data.

The IMAP4 protocol also includes a command continuation mechanism for large data transfers. When a client sends a large message in a literal (data with a known byte count), the server sends a plus-sign continuation request before the client transmits the octets. This prevents ambiguity about where command data ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers each request with tagged responses (success or failure) and also sends information without tags (like a list of new messages) that you should remember.

sections.title: Features and Compatibility
sections.content:
IMAP4 is designed to be upwards compatible with the earlier IMAP2 protocol. The CAPABILITY command advertises which commands and extensions the server supports, allowing clients to discover features like authentication methods or MIME handling.

The protocol supports selective fetching of message parts (via the PARTIAL command) to minimize bandwidth for large messages. The CHECK command asks the server to checkpoint its state (often meaning to flush cached data to disk). The RFC also defines obsolete commands from earlier versions and notes that extensions beyond this specification may be added using the X<atom> syntax for experimental commands.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP4 is backward-compatible with older email protocols. Clients can ask the server what features it supports, and servers can offer experimental features that start with X.

items.title: Tagged Response
items.text: Command completion status with the client's tag (OK, NO, or BAD).

items.title: Untagged Response
items.text: Server data prefixed with * (mailbox status, search results, message data).

items.title: Continuation Request
items.text: Server ready signal prefixed with + for large literal data transfers.

items.title: Initial Greeting
items.text: First response from server (OK, PREAUTH for pre-authenticated, or BYE to reject).
